An analysis of the examples reveals the following rule:

Each input contains several distinct hollow shapes/loops made of a single color.
Inside each hollow shape, a mark (or line) of the same color is added at its center:
- If the hollow interior has an odd width and odd height (i.e. a unique center cell, like $1 \times 1$ or $3 \times 3$), that center cell is filled with the shape's color. (Examples: $3\times 3$ loop with $1\times 1$ center gets that single pixel; $5\times 5$ loop with $3\times 3$ center gets its center pixel; diamond of 5s gets a pixel at its center).
- If the interior dimension is even along an axis, or if an entire central dividing line/cell is filled:
  - For Example 1:
    - 3-shape ($3\times 3$ boundary): interior is $1\times 1$ at (2,2) -> filled.
    - 8-shape ($3\times 5$ boundary, interior $1\times 3$): center of interior is (9,4) -> filled.
    - 2-shape ($5\times 5$ boundary, interior $3\times 3$): center of interior is (4,9) -> filled.
  - For Example 2:
    - Diamond of 5s: interior center at (3,4) -> filled.
    - 9-shape ($5\times 3$ boundary, interior $3\times 1$): wait, in Example 2:
      Rows 7 to 11 (height 5), Cols 8 to 10 (width 3). Interior is at col 9, rows 8, 9, 10.
      In output, row 9 is filled completely! `[9, 9, 9]`. Row 9 was `[9, 0, 9]`, now `[9, 9, 9]`. That's just filling the center pixel at (9,9)!
  - For Example 3:
    - 4-shape ($5\times 5$ boundary, interior $3\times 3$): center of interior is (3,3) -> filled.
    - 6-shape ($3\times 3$ boundary, interior $1\times 1$): center is (3,8) -> filled.
    - 7-shape ($3\times 3$ boundary, interior $1\times 1$): center is (8,2) -> filled.

In all cases, for each shape, find its geometric center (or the center of its bounding box / hollow interior) and set that center pixel to the shape's color!

I am ready for the test input.
